newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Possible players in Russia cabinet reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Possible players in Russia cabinet reshuffle.

text.p: Here are the main players in the Russian government and those who could be affected by a reshuffle urged by President Boris Yeltsin, who says ministers have failed to solve Russia's most pressing social problems.
Former gas industry chief VIKTOR CHERNOMYRDIN, 58, became Russian Prime Minister in December 1992, replacing liberal Yegor Gaidar as a moderate acceptable to reformers and conservatives.

Chernomyrdin's strong backing helped Yeltsin in his struggle against parliamentary opposition in 1993, but he emerged as a strong independent figure during Yeltsin's long absence with illness last year. He could be a presidential candidate in 2000.
Yeltsin has blasted Chernomyrdin for delays in paying wages, pensions and other bills and urged changes to the government team. But the Kremlin has denied persistent rumours that Chernomyrdin may go.

FIRST DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER ALEXEI BOLSHAKOV, 57, is the most senior of three first deputy premiers in the Russian government and spent his working life in the military-industrial complex. But his work is not directly linked to the non-payments crisis and he is unlikely to be part of a reshuffle. He has never been seen as a potential premier.

FIRST DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER VIKTOR ILYUSHIN, 49, has close ties to Yeltsin and is one of the most influential figures in the Kremlin. In Soviet days he worked, like Yeltsin, from the Urals city of Sverdlovsk.
Ilyushin joined the government in August 1996 in charge of social problems, and he is widely rumoured to be among the first in line once the axe starts to fall.
FIRST DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER VLADIMIR POTANIN, 35, was the head of Uneximbank before joining the government and is viewed as a representative of the financial community in the cabinet.
He heads a government commission dealing with non-payments and is also viewed as a possible candidate for dismissal.

FINANCE MINISTER ALEXANDER LIVSHITS, 50, also a deputy prime minister, is widely blamed for delays in wages and pensions, but he argues that he only distributes money allocated in the budget and cannot be held responsible if there is not enough money to go round. He admits he could be in line to go, but says this would hardly help to solve the problem.
DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER AND INTERIOR MINISTER ANATOLY KULIKOV, 50, has just been given responsiblity for tax discipline and cracking down on customs violations.

Kulikov, a hawk in Russia's conflict with rebel Chechnya, controls the Interior Ministry forces and is seen as one of the most powerful figures in government. He seeks more government involvement in the economy and banking sectors but has promised not to use emergency measures while carrying out his duties.

DEFENCE MINSTER IGOR RODIONOV, 60, was appointed last year. Rodionov is loyal to Yeltsin but he seeks more generous funding of the struggling military and has warned that wage delays could lead to the collapse of the armed forces.

KREMLIN CHIEF OF STAFF ANATOLY CHUBAIS, 41, won enemies with a controversial privatisation campaign launched in 1992. He masterminded Yeltsin's successful re-election bid last year and even foes admit he is one of the most talented political managers in Yeltsin's team.

There are rumours he will rejoin the government, perhaps replacing Chernomyrdin as prime minister. But the conservative parliament would never confirm Chubais in office, and this is a gamble even the comabative Yeltsin might not wish to take.

YEGOR STROYEV, 60, is chairman of the Federation Council upper chamber of parliament. A former secretary in charge of agriculture in the Soviet Communist Party's Central Committee, he has made clear that he would work peacefully with Yeltsin and keep his political principles to himself and he has been tipped as a possible candidate for prime minister.

YEGOR GAIDAR, 40, launched Russia's economic reform programme in 1992 and Izvestia newspaper said on Wednesday he might return to the political fray. But there has been no indication that Yeltsin was ready to summon back his old-time ally who has no strong political base or public backing.
